channel.title: h5i Blog
channel.description: Engineering posts on contained development environments for AI coding agents: isolation tiers, egress allowlists, sealed execution receipts, and reviewing work an agent did unattended.

item.title: Teaching an Agent to Use Its Own Box
item.description: The agent skill ships inside the h5i binary, so it cannot document flags the installed binary does not have. Here is what it tells an agent, and how the agent knows it is already inside a box.

item.title: Why the Sandbox Policy Is a File, Not Flags
item.description: A checked-in .h5i/env.toml beats command-line flags for the same reason a Dockerfile beats a shell alias: it is reviewable, versioned, and it can be refused before it runs.

item.title: Write Your First Box Profile
item.description: A step-by-step walkthrough of .h5i/env.toml: pick a tier, grant the paths a build needs, allowlist the registry hosts, declare a dev server, and let the browser reach it.

item.title: Watching a Box's Browser Without Giving It a Port
item.description: The box's stream port is never published. h5i enters the box's network namespace by pid, connects from inside, and hands the socket back out. The terminal viewer binds nothing at all.

item.title: Four Shapes a Box Can Take
item.description: Where the code comes from decides what a box is for and what it is allowed to do. The repo box, the pull-request box, the clone box and the empty box each close a different door.

item.title: Sandboxing AI Agents, Part 3: The Landscape, Compared by Threat Model
item.description: A fair survey of AI agent sandbox approaches: nothing/YOLO, git worktrees, language runtimes, kernel confinement (seccomp + Landlock), containers, gVisor/Kata, Firecracker microVMs, and full VMs. Compared by isolation strength, overhead, setup, and egress control.

item.title: Sandboxing AI Agents, Part 2: Implementing Kernel-Tier Confinement
item.description: How to implement a kernel-tier Linux sandbox for AI agents: probe Landlock/seccomp/namespaces, run a functional self-test, and fail closed instead of silently downgrading.

item.title: Sandboxing AI Agents, Part 4: h5i's Tier Ladder
item.description: h5i's box sandbox is a five-rung ladder (workspace, process, supervised, container, microvm) that matches confinement to trust and to what the host can actually enforce, fail-closed, with every run recorded in a sealed receipt.

item.title: Sandboxing AI Agents, Part 1: Foundations
item.description: AI agent sandboxing from first principles: the threat model (untrusted code, exfiltration, privilege escalation, resource exhaustion) and the Linux primitives (namespaces, seccomp, Landlock, cgroups) that contain it.

item.title: The AI Agent Sandbox With an Output Gate: h5i box
item.description: An AI agent sandbox that holds the code, the toolchain, the dev server and a browser in one boundary. h5i box confines the agent, records what actually ran, and lets nothing out but a patch you reviewed.

item.title: Many Boxes, One Repository
item.description: Running several agents on the same task in parallel needs one thing to be fair: a base that does not move. Boxes pin theirs at creation, which is what makes h5i box compare mean something.

item.title: Who Is Driving the Browser?
item.description: When an agent and a human can both click the same page, something has to arbitrate. h5i's control lock has three rules, and the third one is the one nobody expects.

item.title: Claude Code Hooks vs Git Hooks: Two Lifecycles, Two Trust Models
item.description: Claude Code hooks fire in the agent tool loop; Git hooks fire on repository operations. They see different things and carry different trust guarantees. Here is how to layer both.

item.title: We Built AI Blame, Then Deleted It
item.description: h5i shipped per-line AI provenance: the prompt, the model, the agent, the test result, at every commit boundary. It was cut. Here is what the feature got wrong about the question reviewers were actually asking.

item.title: What Is a Contained Agentic Development Environment?
item.description: A contained agentic development environment holds the code, the coding agent, the toolchain, the dev server and a browser inside one enforced boundary, with nothing of the host inside it and nothing leaving it but a reviewed patch.

item.title: Git Worktrees vs h5i Boxes
item.description: A worktree separates checkouts. A box separates authority. They look similar from the outside and answer different questions, and knowing which one you need takes about thirty seconds.

item.title: How to Track What Claude Code Actually Ran
item.description: Not the prompts. Track the commands: every execution inside the box, its exit code, the lane that observed it, and every destination the egress allowlist refused.

item.title: Making Boxes Start in Seconds, Not Minutes
item.description: Cold dependency install is the difference between a 20-second box and a four-minute one. h5i's cache is keyed by lockfile digest, mounted read-only, and written only by a box with no agent in it.

item.title: Review a Pull Request by Running It
item.description: Reading a diff tells you what someone wrote. Running the branch tells you what it does. h5i box --pr builds and exercises an untrusted pull request in a disposable box, then hands you a report of what actually ran.

item.title: What a Box Copies From Your Claude Code Config, and What It Strips
item.description: A box seeds its own HOME from your agent's real config so it has your settings without racing your files. Credential-shaped entries are dropped at any depth, and transcript stores are pruned for size.

item.title: Reviewing Code an AI Agent Wrote
item.description: When the author is a model that worked unattended, the review order changes. Open what was refused first, then what ran, then the diff, and read the agent's own summary last.

item.title: Why a Diff Is Not Enough for AI-Generated Code
item.description: A diff shows the residue of a process, not the process. For AI-generated code the gap matters: the diff cannot show what ran, what the code reached for, or what a boundary refused. The receipt can.

item.title: What Is Inside an Execution Receipt
item.description: One JSONL record per observed execution: the command, the exit code, the resource usage, the egress verdicts, what the browser saw, and the digest of the policy that was in force. Field by field.

item.title: Triaging a Fleet of Agent Boxes
item.description: One agent branch you can read closely. Thirty is a triage problem. The h5i console counts receipts across five lanes and refuses to turn them into a score, because a number would be the first thing anyone stopped checking.

item.title: The Flight Recorder: Five Lanes and Three Colours
item.description: The h5i console draws one row per receipt across five lanes. Red means the egress allowlist refused a destination. Amber means look at this. Grey means the evidence is weak, which is the most useful thing a dashboard can say.

item.title: Prompt Injection: Contain It, Because You Cannot Detect It
item.description: Detection for prompt injection is low-recall by nature. The durable control is containment: bound what a compromised agent can read, reach and spend, and record every destination the boundary refused.

item.title: CVE-2026-33068: When a Repo's settings.json Decides Trust
item.description: CVE-2026-33068 explained: a committed Claude Code .claude/settings.json could bypass the workspace trust dialog by setting permissions.defaultMode to bypassPermissions. Mechanics, CVSS, and the fix in 2.1.53.

item.title: CVE-2025-59536: Claude Code Trust Dialog Bypass
item.description: CVE-2025-59536 explained: Claude Code before 1.0.111 could execute project code before the startup trust dialog was accepted.

item.title: Pinning What Was Actually Enforced
item.description: A box freezes its base revision and hashes its policy before any state exists on disk, and stamps that digest on every receipt record. Here is why each of those three orderings matters.

item.title: An Audit You Do Not Have to Trust
item.description: Logging is easy and auditing is hard, and the difference is who wrote the record. A workspace is auditable when its evidence is produced outside the thing being audited and stored where that thing cannot reach it.
